claim: ICEclc is an integrative and conjugative element in Pseudomonas that requires development of a transfer competence state in stationary phase.
source: Conjugative transfer of the integrative and conjugative element ICEclc in Pseudomonas requires development of a transfer competence state in stationary phase, which arises only in 3–5% of individual cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known characteristic of ICEclc.

claim: ICEclc transfer competence arises in only 3-5% of individual cells.
source: Conjugative transfer of the integrative and conjugative element ICEclc in Pseudomonas requires development of a transfer competence state in stationary phase, which arises only in 3–5% of individual cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation stated in the abstract and supported by previous work.

claim: An upstream cascade of three consecutive transcription factor-nodes controls transfer competence initiation.
source: Using a variety of genetic tools and epistasis experiments in P. putida, we uncovered an 'upstream' cascade of three consecutive transcription factor-nodes, which controls transfer competence initiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and demonstrated through genetic experiments.

claim: BisR is representative for a new regulator family.
source: One of the uncovered transcription factors (named BisR) is representative for a new regulator family.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis showing no known Pfam domains.

claim: Initiation activates a feedback loop controlled by a heteromeric transcription factor named BisDC.
source: Initiation activates a feedback loop, controlled by a second hitherto unrecognized heteromeric transcription factor named BisDC.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through genetic and modeling experiments.

claim: The feedback loop acts as a scalable converter of unimodal (analog) input to bistable (digital) output.
source: Stochastic modelling and experimental data demonstrated the feedback loop to act as a scalable converter of unimodal (population-wide or 'analog') input to bistable (subpopulation-specific or 'digital') output.
evidence: This is demonstrated through both stochastic modeling and experimental validation in the study.

claim: The feedback loop enables prolonged production of BisDC.
source: The feedback loop further enables prolonged production of BisDC, which ensures expression of the 'downstream' functions mediating ICE transfer competence in activated cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by modeling results showing sustained BisDC levels.

claim: The ICEclc regulatory constellation with BisR and BisDC is widespread among Gamma- and Beta-proteobacteria.
source: Phylogenetic analyses showed that the ICEclc regulatory constellation with BisR and BisDC is widespread among Gamma- and Beta-proteobacteria, including various pathogenic strains, highlighting its evolutionary conservation and prime importance to control the behaviour of this wide family of conjugative elements.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in the results.

claim: Biological bistability refers to the existence of two mutually exclusive stable states within a population of genetically identical individuals.
source: Biological bistability refers to the existence of two mutually exclusive stable states within a population of genetically identical individuals, leading to two distinct phenotypes or developmental programs (Shu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a definition provided with citation to support the concept.

claim: Bistability has been considered as a bet-hedging strategy leading to increased fitness.
source: Bistability has been considered as a bet-hedging strategy leading to an increased fitness of the genotype by ensuring survival of one of both phenotypes depending on environmental conditions (Veening et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work on bistability.

claim: ICEclc is maintained in the integrated state in the majority of cells.
source: In the majority of cells ICEclc is maintained in the integrated state, but a small proportion of cells (3–5%) in stationary phase activates the ICE transfer competence program (Minoia et al., 2008; Delavat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work characterizing ICEclc behavior.

claim: Transfer competent cells excise and replicate the ICE upon resuming growth.
source: Upon resuming growth, transfer competent (tc) donor cells excise and replicate the ICE (Delavat et al., 2019), which can conjugate to a recipient cell, where the ICE can integrate (Delavat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on ICEclc transfer.

claim: ICEclc transfer competence comprises a differentiated stable state.
source: ICEclc transfer competence comprises a differentiated stable state, because initiated tc cells do not transform back to the ICE-quiescent state.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the transfer competence state.

claim: Transfer competent cells eventually arrest division completely.
source: Although tc cells divide a few times, their division is compromised by the ICE and eventually arrests completely (Takano et al., 2019; Reinhard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work on tc cell behavior.

claim: The core region of ICEclc is higher expressed in stationary than exponential phase cultures grown on 3-chlorobenzoate.
source: Transcriptomic studies indicated that the core region of ICEclc (Figure 1A) is higher expressed in stationary than exponential phase cultures grown on 3-chlorobenzoate (3-CBA), and organized in at least half a dozen transcriptional units (Gaillard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous transcriptomic work.

claim: A group of three consecutive regulatory genes precludes ICEclc activation in exponentially growing cells.
source: A group of three consecutive regulatory genes precludes ICEclc activation in exponentially growing cells, with the first gene (mfsR) constituting a negative autoregulatory feedback (Figure 1B; Pradervand et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work on ICEclc regulation.

claim: Overexpression of tciR leads to a dramatic increase of the proportion of cells activating the ICEclc transfer competence program.
source: Overexpression of the most distal of the three genes (tciR), leads to a dramatic increase of the proportion of cells activating the ICEclc transfer competence program (Pradervand et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work and confirmed in this study.

claim: Inducing tciR expression by IPTG addition triggered ICEclc transfer from succinate-grown cells up to frequencies close to those observed under wild-type growth conditions with 3-CBA.
source: In contrast, inducing tciR expression by IPTG addition triggered ICEclc transfer from succinate-grown cells up to frequencies close to those observed under wild-type growth conditions with 3-CBA (Miyazaki and van der Meer, 2011b) (10–2 transconjugant colony-forming units (CFU) per donor CFU, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transfer of wild-type ICEclc from succinate-grown P. putida to an ICEclc-free isogenic P. putida was below detection limit in absence of cloned tciR.
source: In absence of cloned tciR, transfer of wild-type ICEclc from succinate-grown P. putida to an ICEclc-free isogenic P. putida was below detection limit, indicating that spontaneous ICE activation under those conditions is negligible (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Induction of tciR from pMEtciR in P. putida without ICEclc was insufficient to trigger eGFP production from a single-copy Pint promoter.
source: Induction of tciR from pMEtciR in P. putida without ICEclc was insufficient to trigger eGFP production from a single-copy Pint promoter, which is a hallmark of induction of ICEclc transfer competence (Figure 2B; Minoia et al., 2008; Delavat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In presence of ICEclc, induction of tciR yielded a clear increased subpopulation of activated cells.
source: In contrast, in presence of ICEclc, similar induction of tciR yielded a clear increased subpopulation of activated cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TciR does not directly activate Pint, but only through one or more other ICE-located factors.
source: This suggested, therefore, that TciR does not directly activate Pint, but only through one or more other ICE-located factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing TciR cannot activate Pint without ICE.

claim: The PbisR-egfp fusion was activated upon induction of TciR compared to a vector-only control.
source: In contrast, the PbisR-egfp fusion was activated upon induction of TciR compared to a vector-only control (p=0.0042, paired t-test, Figure 2B & D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with statistical significance shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: The link between TciR and ICEclc transfer competence proceeds through transcription activation of the promoter upstream of the gene bisR.
source: This suggested that the link between TciR and ICEclc transfer competence proceeds through transcription activation of the promoter upstream of the gene bisR (previously designated orf101284).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that TciR activates PbisR.

claim: bisR is predicted to encode a 251-aa protein of unknown function with no detectable Pfam-domains.
source: bisR is predicted to encode a 251-aa protein of unknown function with no detectable Pfam-domains.
evidence: This is stated based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Structural analysis using Phyre2 suggested three putative domains in BisR with low confidence.
source: Further structural analysis using Phyre2 (Kelley et al., 2015) suggested three putative domains with low confidence (between 38% and 53%, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated based on computational structural prediction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: BisR has a predicted DNA-binding domain.
source: One of these is a predicted DNA-binding domain, which hinted at the possible function of BisR as a transcriptional regulator itself.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: BisR homologs are widely distributed and well conserved among Beta-, Alpha- and Gammaproteobacteria.
source: BlastP analysis showed that BisR homologs are widely distributed and well conserved among Beta-, Alpha- and Gammaproteobacteria, with homologies ranging from 43–100% amino acid identity over the (quasi) full sequence length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated based on BlastP analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inducing bisR by IPTG addition from Ptac triggered high rates of ICEclc transfer on succinate media.
source: Inducing bisR by IPTG addition from Ptac triggered high rates of ICEclc transfer on succinate media (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Deletion of bisR on ICEclc abolished its transfer, even upon overexpression of tciR.
source: Deletion of bisR on ICEclc abolished its transfer, even upon overexpression of tciR, but could be restored upon ectopic expression of bisR (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A demonstrating epistasis.

claim: Transfer of an ICEclc deleted for tciR could be restored by ectopic bisR expression.
source: In addition, transfer of an ICEclc deleted for tciR (Pradervand et al., 2014) could be restored by ectopic bisR expression (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A demonstrating epistasis.

claim: TciR is upstream in the regulatory cascade of BisR.
source: This indicated that TciR is 'upstream' in the regulatory cascade of BisR, and that TciR does not act anywhere else on the expression of components crucial for ICEclc transfer.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis experiments showing bisR can bypass tciR deletion.

claim: IPTG induction of bisR in P. putida without ICE did not yield activation of the single-copy Pint or PinR transcriptional reporter fusions.
source: IPTG induction of bisR in P. putida without ICE again did not yield activation of the single-copy Pint or PinR transcriptional reporter fusions, whereas some repression was observed on Pint itself (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BisR induction in P. putida UWC1 with ICEclc led to a massive activation of Pint and PinR reporters in virtually all cells.
source: In contrast, BisR induction in P. putida UWC1 with ICEclc led to a massive activation of the same reporter constructs in virtually all cells (Figure 3C), compared to a vector-only control (Figure 2C, pME6032).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: BisR is an intermediate regulator between TciR and further factors encoded downstream of the alpA-promoter.
source: This suggested that BisR was an(other) intermediate regulator step in the complete cascade of activation of ICEclc transfer competence.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing BisR cannot directly activate Pint/PinR without ICE.

claim: BisR induction triggered very strong expression from a single copy PalpA–egfp transcriptional fusion in all cells.
source: Of the tested ICE–promoters within this 7 kb region, BisR induction triggered very strong expression from a single copy PalpA–egfp transcriptional fusion in all cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3D.

claim: BisR is a transcription activator.
source: This indicated that BisR is a transcription activator, and an intermediate regulator between TciR and further factors encoded downstream of the alpA-promoter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that BisR activates PalpA.

claim: Cloning the genes from alpA to inrR on plasmid under control of Ptac and inducing with IPTG resulted in activation of PinR–egfp and Pint–echerry expression in P. putida without ICEclc.
source: Cloning the genes from alpA all the way to inrR (Figure 1A) on plasmid pME6032 under control of Ptac and inducing that construct with IPTG resulted in activation of PinR–egfp and Pint–echerry expression in P. putida without ICEclc (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: One or more regulatory factors directly controlling expression of PinR and/or Pint are encoded in the alpA to inrR region.
source: This indicated that one or more regulatory factors directly controlling expression of PinR and/or Pint were encoded in this region, which we tried to identify by subcloning different gene configurations.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that the alpA-inrR region can activate Pint/PinR.

claim: Removing alpA from the initial construct had no measurable effect on expression of the fluorescent reporters.
source: Removing alpA from the initial construct had no measurable effect on expression of the fluorescent reporters, but replacing Ptac by the native PalpA promoter abolished all Pint reporter activation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PalpA is silent without activation by BisR.
source: This suggested that PalpA is silent without activation by BisR (see below) and no spontaneous production of regulatory factors occurred.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that PalpA does not drive expression without BisR.

claim: Neither bisC or bisD alone, but only the combination of bisDC resulted in reporter expression from Pint in P. putida UWC1 without ICEclc.
source: Neither bisC or bisD alone, but only the combination of bisDC resulted in reporter expression from Pint in P. putida UWC1 without ICEclc (Figure 4B), and similarly, of PinR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inducing either bisC or bisD from a plasmid yielded a small proportion of cells expressing the Pint reporters in the presence of ICEclc.
source: In the presence of ICEclc, inducing either bisC or bisD from a plasmid yielded a small proportion of cells expressing the Pint reporters (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Induction of bisDC in combination caused a majority of cells to express fluorescence from Pint in P. putida containing ICEclc.
source: In contrast, induction of bisDC in combination caused a majority of cells to express fluorescence from Pint in P. putida containing ICEclc (Figure 4C) or ICEclc-∆bisD (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: BisDC acts as an ensemble to activate transcription.
source: These results indicated that BisDC acts as an ensemble to activate transcription, and this pointed to bisDC as the last step in the regulatory cascade, since it was the minimum unit sufficient for activation of the Pint–promoter, which is exclusively expressed in the subpopulation of tc cells of wild-type P. putida with ICEclc (Delavat et al., 2016; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing both subunits are required for activity.

claim: Induction of bisDC from plasmid pMEbisDC yielded high frequencies of ICEclc transfer from P. putida UWC1 under succinate-growth conditions.
source: Induction of bisDC from plasmid pMEbisDC yielded high frequencies of ICEclc transfer from P. putida UWC1 under succinate-growth conditions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Expression of BisDC induced transfer of ICEclc-variants deleted for tciR or for bisR.
source: Expression of BisDC also induced transfer of ICEclc-variants deleted for tciR or for bisR (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4D demonstrating epistasis.

claim: Both tciR and bisR relay activation steps to PbisR and PalpA, respectively, but not to further downstream ICE promoters.
source: This confirmed that both tciR and bisR relay activation steps to PbisR and PalpA, respectively, but not to further downstream ICE promoters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis experiments showing BisDC can bypass tciR and bisR deletions.

claim: An ICEclc deleted for bisD could not be restored for transfer by overexpression of tciR or bisR, but only by complementation with bisDC.
source: Moreover, an ICEclc deleted for bisD could not be restored for transfer by overexpression of tciR or bisR, but only by complementation with bisDC (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4D demonstrating epistasis.

claim: The frequency of transfer of an ICEclc lacking bisD complemented by expression of bisDC in trans was two orders of magnitude lower than that of similarly complemented wild-type ICEclc.
source: Interestingly, the frequency of transfer of an ICEclc lacking bisD complemented by expression of bisDC in trans was two orders of magnitude lower than that of similarly complemented wild-type ICEclc, ICEclc with tciR- or bisR-deletion (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is a necessity of some 'reinforcement' occurring in the wild-type configuration that is lacking in the bisD deletion and cannot be restored by in trans induction of plasmid-cloned bisDC.
source: This was similar as the reduction in reporter expression observed in P. putida ICEclc-∆bisD complemented with pMEbisDC compared to wild-type ICEclc (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and suggested the necessity of some 'reinforcement' occurring in the wild-type configuration that was lacking in the bisD deletion and could not be restored by in trans induction of plasmid-cloned bisDC.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation of reduced transfer in bisD deletion complemented in trans.

claim: Induction by IPTG of the plasmid-cloned fragment encompassing the gene region parA-shi-bisDC caused strong activation of reporter gene expression from PalpA in P. putida without ICEclc.
source: Induction by IPTG of the plasmid-cloned fragment encompassing the gene region parA-shi-bisDC caused strong activation of reporter gene expression from PalpA in P. putida without ICEclc (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The minimal region that still maintained PalpA induction encompassed bisDC, although much lower than with a cloned parA-shi-bisDC fragment.
source: The minimal region that still maintained PalpA induction encompassed bisDC, although much lower than with a cloned parA-shi-bisDC fragment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When the parA-shi-bisDC fragment was extended by alpA itself, reporter expression from PalpA was abolished.
source: Interestingly, when the parA-shi-bisDC fragment was extended by alpA itself, reporter expression from PalpA was abolished, whereas also a fragment containing only alpA caused significant repression of the alpA promoter (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The alpA gene is predicted to encode a 70-amino acid DNA binding protein with homology to phage regulators.
source: The alpA gene is predicted to encode a 70-amino acid DNA binding protein with homology to phage regulators (Trempy et al., 1994; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated based on bioinformatic analysis with citation.

claim: The feedback loop consists of a positive forward part that includes BisDC and a modulatory repressive branch including AlpA.
source: The feedback loop, therefore, seemed to consist of a positive forward part that includes BisDC (reinforced by an as yet unknown other mechanism) and a modulatory repressive branch including AlpA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of BisDC activation and AlpA repression of PalpA.

claim: Induction of BisDC was sufficient for activation of transcription from PalpA, but effectively only yielded a small subpopulation of cells with high reporter fluorescence values.
source: Although induction of BisDC was sufficient for activation of transcription from PalpA, this effectively only yielded a small subpopulation of cells with high reporter fluorescence values (Figure 5B & C), in contrast to induction of the larger cloned gene region encompassing parA-shi-bisDC that activated all cells (Figure 5B & C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Simulation of a BisDC feedback loop with an arbitrary start of binomially distributed BisDC quantities yielded a bimodal population with two BisDC output states after 100 time steps.
source: Stochastic simulations (n = 10,000) of this bare feedback loop with an arbitrary start of binomially distributed BisDC quantities (mean = 8 molecules per cell, Figure 6B, INPUT), yielded a bimodal population with two BisDC output states after 100 time steps, one of which is zero (black bar in histograms) and the other with a mean positive BisDC value (magenta) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from stochastic modeling shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The proportion of cells with output zero from the BisDC loop is dependent on the binding and unbinding constants of BisDC to the alpA promoter, and the BisDC degradation rate.
source: Parameter variation showed that the proportion of cells with output zero from the loop is dependent on the binding and unbinding constants of BisDC to the alpA promoter, and the BisDC degradation rate (Figure 6B, different A1, A2 and A4-values).
evidence: This is a result from parameter variation in stochastic modeling shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A BisDC feedback loop can produce bimodal output, once BisDC is present.
source: This simulation thus indicated that a BisDC feedback loop can produce bimodal output, once BisDC is present.
evidence: This is concluded from the stochastic modeling results.

claim: Activation by BisR only influences the proportion of zero and positive BisDC states in the population, but not the mean resulting BisDC quantity in cells with positive state.
source: Increasing the (uniformly distributed) mean quantity of BisR in the simulations, within a per-cell range that is typically measured for transcription factors (Li et al., 2014), increased the proportion of cells with positive BisDC state, but did not influence their mean BisDC quantity (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from stochastic modeling shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Simulation of the full regulatory hierarchy showed that bimodality already appeared at the level of BisR.
source: Simulation of this configuration showed that bimodality already appeared at the level of BisR (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a result from stochastic modeling shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Simulations of an architecture without the BisDC feedback loop consistently resulted in lower protein output from BisDC–regulated promoters in activated cells than with feedback.
source: Importantly, simulations of an architecture without the BisDC feedback loop consistently resulted in lower protein output from BisDC–regulated promoters in activated cells than with feedback (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a result from stochastic modeling shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The ICE regulatory network converts unimodal or stochastic ('analog') expression of TciR and BisR among all cells to a consistent subpopulation of cells with positive ('digital') BisDC state.
source: This suggests two crucial functions for the ICE regulatory network: first, to convert unimodal or stochastic ('analog') expression of TciR and BisR among all cells to a consistent subpopulation of cells with positive ('digital') BisDC state, and secondly, to ensure sufficient BisDC levels to activate downstream promoters within the positive cell population (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is concluded from the stochastic modeling results.

claim: The ICE regulatory network ensures sufficient BisDC levels to activate downstream promoters within the positive cell population.
source: This suggests two crucial functions for the ICE regulatory network: first, to convert unimodal or stochastic ('analog') expression of TciR and BisR among all cells to a consistent subpopulation of cells with positive ('digital') BisDC state, and secondly, to ensure sufficient BisDC levels to activate downstream promoters within the positive cell population (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is concluded from the stochastic modeling results.

claim: Induction from Ptac by IPTG addition yields unimodal (analog) production of BisR, the mean level of which can be controlled by the IPTG concentration.
source: Induction from Ptac by IPTG addition yields unimodal (analog) production of BisR, the mean level of which can be controlled by the IPTG concentration (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of all components of the system, IPTG induction of BisR led to bistable activation of both reporters.
source: In the presence of all components of the system, IPTG induction of BisR led to bistable activation of both reporters (Figure 7B, ABC).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: The proportion of fluorescent cells was in line with predictions from stochastic simulations as a function of the relative strength of Ptac activation.
source: The proportion of fluorescent cells was in line with predictions from stochastic simulations as a function of the relative strength of Ptac activation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and model predictions shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The median fluorescence of activated cells remained the same at different IPTG (and thus BisR) concentrations.
source: Furthermore, in agreement with model predictions (Figure 6C), the median fluorescence of activated cells remained the same at different IPTG (and thus BisR) concentrations (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 7E that agrees with model predictions.

claim: The feedback loop architecture transforms a unimodal (analog) regulatory factor concentration (BisR) into a stabilized bimodal (digital) output.
source: These results confirmed that the feedback loop architecture transforms a unimodal (analog) regulatory factor concentration (BisR) into a stabilized bimodal (digital) output.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental validation of the analog-to-digital converter.

claim: BisC carries a DUF2857-domain.
source: Pfam analysis detected a DUF2857-domain in the BisC protein, and further structural analysis using Phyre2 indicated significant similarities of BisC to FlhC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated based on Pfam analysis.

claim: BisC has significant similarities to FlhC.
source: Pfam analysis detected a DUF2857-domain in the BisC protein, and further structural analysis using Phyre2 indicated significant similarities of BisC to FlhC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated based on structural analysis using Phyre2.

claim: FlhC is a subunit of the master flagellar activator FlhDC of E. coli and Salmonella.
source: FlhC is a subunit of the master flagellar activator FlhDC of E. coli and Salmonella (Claret and Hughes, 2000; Liu and Matsumura, 1994).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: BisD carries a ParB domain, with a predicted DNA binding domain in the C-terminal portion of the protein.
source: BisD carries a ParB domain, with a predicted DNA binding domain in the C-terminal portion of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated based on domain analysis.

claim: bisDC loci are widespread among pathogenic and environmental Gamma- and Beta-proteobacteria, and are also found in some Alphaproteobacteria.
source: Database searches showed that bisDC loci are also widespread among pathogenic and environmental Gamma- and Beta-proteobacteria, and are also found in some Alphaproteobacteria (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated based on database searches shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Several genomes contained more than one bisDC homolog, the most extreme case being Bordetella petrii DSM12804 with up to four homologs belonging to four different clades.
source: Several genomes contained more than one bisDC homolog, the most extreme case being Bordetella petrii DSM12804 with up to four homologs belonging to four different clades (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The gene synteny from bisR to inrR of ICEclc was maintained in several genomes.
source: The gene synteny from bisR to inrR of ICEclc was maintained in several genomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting them being part of related ICEs with similar regulatory architecture.
evidence: This is stated based on comparative genomics shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Regions of high similarity to the ICEclc regulatory core extended to the well-known pathogenicity islands of the PAGI-2 and PAGI-16 families.
source: Notably, some of those are opportunistic pathogens, such as P. aeruginosa, B. petrii, B. bronchiseptica, or X. citri, and regions of high similarity to the ICEclc regulatory core extended to the well-known pathogenicity islands of the PAGI-2 (Klockgether et al., 2007) and PAGI-16 families (Hong et al., 2016; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated based on comparative genomics with citations.

claim: Several of the ICEclc core homologs carry genes suspected in virulence.
source: Several of the ICEclc core homologs carry genes suspected in virulence (e.g., filamentous hemagglutinin [Sun et al., 2016] encoded on the P. aeruginosa HS9 and Carb01-63 genomic islands), or implicated in acquired antibiotic resistance (e.g, multidrug efflux pump on the A. xylosoxidans NH44784-1996 element (Miyazaki et al., 2015), and carbapenem resistance on the PAGI-16 elements [Hong et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is stated based on comparative genomics with citations.

claim: The decision for horizontal transfer is costly and potentially damages the host cell.
source: The decision for horizontal transfer is costly and potentially damages the host cell (Delavat et al., 2016; Pradervand et al., 2014), which is probably why its frequency of occurrence in most ICEs is fairly low (<10–5 per cell in a host cell population) (Delavat et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The frequency of occurrence of horizontal transfer in most ICEs is fairly low (<10–5 per cell in a host cell population).
source: The decision for horizontal transfer is costly and potentially damages the host cell (Delavat et al., 2016; Pradervand et al., 2014), which is probably why its frequency of occurrence in most ICEs is fairly low (<10–5 per cell in a host cell population) (Delavat et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: The mechanisms that initiate and ensure ICE horizontal transfer must have been selected to operate under extremely low opportunity with high success.
source: Consequently, the mechanisms that initiate and ensure ICE horizontal transfer must have been selected to operate under extremely low opportunity with high success.
evidence: This is inferred from the low frequency but importance of ICE transfer.

claim: ICEclc transfer competence is initiated in cells during stationary phase conditions.
source: ICEclc is further particular in the sense that its transfer competence is initiated in cells during stationary phase conditions (Miyazaki et al., 2012), which restricts global transcription and activity, and may even profoundly alter the cytoplasmic state of the cell (Parry et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The basis for initiation and maintenance of ICEclc transfer competence in a minority of cells originates in a multinode regulatory network that includes a positive feedback loop.
source: The results of our work here reveal that the basis for initiation and maintenance of ICEclc transfer competence in a minority of cells in a stationary phase population (Reinhard et al., 2013), originates in a multinode regulatory network that further includes a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The network consists of regulatory factors MfsR, TciR, BisR and BisDC, acting sequentially on singular or multiple nodes.
source: Genetic dissection, epistasis experiments and expression of individual components in P. putida devoid of the ICE showed that the network consists of a number of regulatory factors, composed of MfsR, TciR, BisR and BisDC, acting sequentially on singular (TciR, BisR) or multiple nodes (BisDC).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental results.

claim: The network has an 'upstream' branch controlling the initiation of transfer competence, a 'bistability generator' that confines the input signal, and maintains the 'downstream' path of transfer competence to a dedicated subpopulation of cells.
source: The network has an 'upstream' branch controlling the initiation of transfer competence, a 'bistability generator' that confines the input signal, and maintains the 'downstream' path of transfer competence to a dedicated subpopulation of cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The mfsR-marR-tciR operon is probably the main break on activation of the upstream branch.
source: The previously characterized mfsR-marR-tciR operon (Pradervand et al., 2014), whose transcription is controlled through autorepression by MfsR, is probably the main break on activation of the upstream branch.
evidence: This is inferred from previous work and the current results on the regulatory cascade.

claim: Autorepression by MfsR in wild-type ICEclc results in low unimodal transcription from PmfsR and therefore, likely, to low TciR levels in all cells.
source: Autorepression by MfsR in wild-type ICEclc results in low unimodal transcription from PmfsR (Pradervand et al., 2014) and therefore, likely, to low TciR levels in all cells.
evidence: This is stated with citation and inference about TciR levels.

claim: TciR appeared as a weak activator of the bisR promoter.
source: TciR appeared here as a weak activator of the bisR promoter, suggesting that only in a small proportion of cells it manages to trigger bisR transcription, as our model simulations further attested.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by modeling.

claim: BisR was a very potent activator of its target, the alpA promoter.
source: In contrast to TciR, BisR was a very potent activator of its target, the alpA promoter.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of strong PalpA activation by BisR.

claim: BisR triggers and transmits the response in a scalable manner to the bistability generator.
source: Model simulations suggested that BisR triggers and transmits the response in a scalable manner to the bistability generator, encoded by the genes downstream of PalpA.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results.

claim: BisDC production was sufficient to activate the previously characterized bistable ICEclc promoters Pint and PinR.
source: BisDC production was sufficient to activate the previously characterized bistable ICEclc promoters Pint and PinR, making it the key regulator for the 'downstream' branch (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results showing BisDC activates Pint and PinR.

claim: BisDC was part of a feedback mechanism activating transcription from PalpA, and therefore, regulates its own production.
source: Importantly, BisDC was also part of a feedback mechanism activating transcription from PalpA, and therefore, regulates its own production.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results showing BisDC activates PalpA.

claim: ICEclc transfer competence regulatory architecture has two states, one of which is zero (inactive) and the other with a positive value (activation of transfer competence).
source: Mathematically speaking, the ICEclc transfer competence regulatory architecture has two states, one of which is zero (inactive) and the other with a positive value (activation of transfer competence).
evidence: This is a mathematical characterization of the bistable system.

claim: Stochastic modelling suggested that the feedback loop maintains positive output during a longer time period than in its absence.
source: Stochastic modelling suggested that the feedback loop maintains positive output during a longer time period than in its absence (although it will drop to zero at infinite time).
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results.

claim: Transfer competent cells do not return to a silent ICEclc state, but become irreparably damaged, arrest their division and wither.
source: Previous experimental data suggested that the tc cells indeed do not return to a silent ICEclc state, but become irreparably damaged, arrest their division (Takano et al., 2019) and wither (Reinhard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: Because transfer competent cells are proportionally low in number, there is no fitness cost on the population carrying the ICE.
source: However, because their number is proportionally low, there is no fitness cost on the population carrying the ICE (Delavat et al., 2016; Gaillard et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The advantage of prolonged feedback output is that constant levels of the BisCD regulator can be maintained, allowing coordinated and organized production of the components necessary for the ICEclc transfer itself.
source: The advantage of prolonged feedback output seems that constant levels of the BisCD regulator can be maintained, allowing coordinated and organized production of the components necessary for the ICEclc transfer itself.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling and experimental results.

claim: The feedback loop may have a critical role to ensure faithful completion of the transfer competence pathway during stationary phase.
source: Because Pseudomonas cells activate ICEclc transfer competence upon entry in stationary phase, the feedback loop may have a critical role to ensure faithful completion of the transfer competence pathway during this period of limiting nutrients, and to allow the ICE to excise and transfer from tc cells once new nutrients become available (Delavat et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculated based on the timing of ICEclc activation and the function of the feedback loop.

claim: Deletions in the gene inrR drastically decreased ICEclc transfer capability by 45-fold and reduced reporter gene expression from Pint.
source: For example, we previously found that deletions in the gene inrR drastically decreased ICEclc transfer capability by 45–fold and reduced reporter gene expression from Pint (Minoia et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of InrR alone did not show any direct activation of Pint, PinR or PalpA, and InrR is thus unlikely to be a direct transcription activator protein.
source: Expression of InrR alone, however, did not show any direct activation of Pint, PinR or PalpA, and InrR is thus unlikely to be a direct transcription activator protein.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results in this study.

claim: Induction of AlpA may repress output from the PalpA promoter, and modulate the feedback loop that is initiated by BisR and maintained by BisDC.
source: Our results also indicated that induction of AlpA may repress output from the PalpA promoter, and modulate the feedback loop that is initiated by BisR and maintained by BisDC.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results showing AlpA repression.

claim: Induction of bisDC was sufficient to activate expression from PalpA, but it was enhanced through an as yet uncharacterized mechanism involving its upstream regions.
source: Furthermore, although induction of bisDC was sufficient to activate expression from PalpA, it was enhanced through an as yet uncharacterized mechanism involving its upstream regions.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results showing enhanced activation with upstream regions.

claim: The stationary phase sigma factor RpoS may be important for other ICEclc regulatory promoters.
source: Previous results also highlighted the implication of the stationary phase sigma factor RpoS for PinR activation (Figure 1B; Miyazaki et al., 2012), which may be more generally important for other ICEclc regulatory promoters as well.
evidence: This is stated with citation and speculation about broader role.

claim: The different ICEclc regulatory loci (i.e., bisR-alpA-bisDC-inrR) are widely conserved in Beta- and Gammaproteobacteria.
source: Phylogenetic analyses showed the different ICEclc regulatory loci (i.e., bisR-alpA-bisDC-inrR) to be widely conserved in Beta- and Gammaproteobacteria, with only few small variations in regulatory gene configurations.
evidence: This is stated based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: These regions are most likely part of ICEclc-like elements in these organisms.
source: Most likely, these regions are part of ICEclc-like elements in these organisms, several of which have been detected previously (Miyazaki et al., 2015; Miyazaki, 2011a; Gaillard et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation and previous detection of similar elements.

claim: ICEclc regulatory loci are part of PAGI-2 and PAGI-16 family genomic islands in P. aeruginosa clinical isolates that have been implicated in the distribution of virulence factors and antibiotic resistance elements.
source: They are further part of PAGI-2 (Klockgether et al., 2007) and PAGI-16 family genomic islands in P. aeruginosa clinical isolates (Hong et al., 2016) that have been implicated in the distribution of virulence factors and antibiotic resistance elements.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work.

claim: The ICEclc regulatory cascade for transfer competence is widely conserved, controlling horizontal dissemination of this important class of bacterial conjugative elements.
source: The ICEclc regulatory cascade for transfer competence thus seems widely conserved, controlling horizontal dissemination of this important class of bacterial conjugative elements.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the phylogenetic analysis.
